title: Everyone in one room, once
where: ESM, Kirchberg — B-2.04, the long room with the ceiling-tile camera

lines.text: Twenty-one people, one room, 09:30 to 12:30. The agenda went out on the second of April with the Charter attached, and at 09:34 four of them are reading it for the first time. Legal are on video from the fourth floor, on the camera that has pointed at the ceiling tiles since the EFSF migration.
lines.plain: Twenty-one people are in one room, booked from 09:30 to 12:30. The agenda was sent on 2 April with the Project Charter attached. At 09:34, four people are reading it for the first time. Legal join by video from the fourth floor, on the camera that has pointed at the ceiling tiles since the EFSF migration.
g: Meeting Agenda
the list of points, times and owners sent out before a meeting
Planning Kick-off Meeting
the formal meeting that opens the Planning Phase for the whole project team
ref: Send out the Meeting Agenda in advance.

lines.text: Notes or minutes?
lines.plain: Do you want me to take informal notes, or official minutes?

lines.text: Minutes. And mark the actions while you hear them, because I will lose four of them by eleven.
lines.plain: Official minutes. Please write down each action item as you hear it. If you wait, I will forget about four of them by 11:00.
ref: Ensure a minute-taker is identified to make notes identifying action items.

lines.text: Then I record who is here. Not who was invited. Finance and Control have sent a deputy and I do not have her name.
lines.plain: Then I will record the people who are actually present, not the people who were invited. Finance and Control sent a deputy, and I do not know her name.

lines.text: Names first. Each of you, one sentence on what CASTOR changes about your Tuesday.
lines.plain: We start with introductions. Please each say your name and one sentence about how CASTOR will change your normal working Tuesday.
ref: Introduce the meeting participants.

lines.text: Twenty-one sentences.
lines.plain: That will be twenty-one sentences.

lines.text: Fifteen minutes. It is the cheapest fifteen minutes of the morning.
lines.plain: It will take fifteen minutes. It is the most useful fifteen minutes we will spend today.

lines.text: It takes nineteen. A tester from IT says CASTOR will change nothing about his Tuesday, which turns out to be the most useful sentence anybody says before the break.
lines.plain: It takes nineteen minutes. A tester from the IT division says CASTOR will change nothing about his Tuesday. That turns out to be the most useful sentence anyone says before the break.

lines.text: Fourteen years old. Fourteen hundred payment fields re-keyed by hand every quarter. Three working days to reconcile a disbursement. Two open audit findings with my signature on the response to both.
lines.plain: The LOS system is fourteen years old. Staff retype 1,400 payment fields by hand every three months. Checking the records after a payment takes three working days. There are two open audit findings, and I signed the reply to both.

lines.text: I am not here for a nicer system. I am here to stop writing those responses.
lines.plain: I do not want a nicer system. I want to stop writing replies to audit findings.

lines.text: Charter, line by line. Scope. SC1 to SC5. Eight point four million, three thousand one hundred person-days, twenty-six months, go-live the fifteenth of May 2028.
lines.plain: Now I go through the Project Charter line by line. The scope. The five success criteria. The budget of 8.4 million euro, the 3,100 person-days of effort, the 26 months, and the go-live date of 15 May 2028.
ref: Walk the participants through the Project Charter so they understand the project scope.

lines.text: Stop at SC1. Five working days down to one. Those five days are not idle. Somebody checks the drawdown schedule against the loan agreement, somebody else releases the instruction, and they are never the same person. So tell me who does the checking inside your one day.
lines.plain: Stop at SC1. It says five working days must become one. Those five days are not wasted. One person checks the drawdown schedule against the loan agreement. A different person releases the payment instruction. They are never the same person. So tell me who does that checking inside your single day.
g: drawdown schedule
the agreed plan of when a borrower may take each part of a loan

lines.text: I do not know yet.
lines.plain: I do not know the answer yet.

lines.text: It goes on the sheet as an assumption to be tested. Not as an argument I intend to win this morning.
lines.plain: I will write it down as an assumption that we must test. I will not treat it as an argument to win today.
ref: Discuss risks, constraints and assumptions.

lines.text: Three boxes. Steering Committee, Business Implementation Group, Core Team. Everyone here is in one of them and I will tell you which before lunch.
lines.plain: There are three groups: the Project Steering Committee, the Business Implementation Group and the Project Core Team. Everyone in this room belongs to one of them, and I will say which one before lunch.
g: Project Core Team
the specialists who build the deliverables, coordinated by the Project Manager
ref: Describe and discuss the project roles and responsibilities.

lines.text: On approach. We buy this platform. We do not build it.
lines.plain: About the approach. We will buy this platform. We will not build it ourselves.

lines.text: You have said that four times since March.
lines.plain: You have said that four times since March.

lines.text: And I will say it in September, when somebody in my own division proposes we build it. Minute it, Henry.
lines.plain: And I will say it again in September, when somebody from my own division suggests we build it. Henry, please record it in the minutes.

lines.text: Before the plans. The collateral register report — the two pages of lessons learned. One page is about business experts promised part-time.
lines.plain: One thing before we discuss the plans. There is a report from the collateral register project, with two pages of lessons learned. One whole page is about business experts who were promised part-time.
ref: At this early stage, past experiences, and especially Lessons Learned from previous similar projects, will significantly help the project team.

lines.text: Which is why item eight is the list of plans this project actually needs. Whatever we settle on lands in the Handbook, and the Handbook is the thing you will be held to.
lines.plain: That is why item eight on the agenda is the list of plans this project really needs. Whatever we agree goes into the Project Handbook, and the Handbook is the document that will hold you to it.
ref: Discuss the project plans needed for the project. The final set of required project plans will be documented in the Project Handbook.

lines.text: Then I want my half hour on the quarterly interest notices. Four hundred letters a quarter, merged in Word, checked twice, posted by a human being. Worst job in the division, and it reads the same loan data CASTOR will hold.
lines.plain: Then I want half an hour on the quarterly interest notices. We send 400 letters every three months. They are merged in Word, checked twice, and posted by a person. It is the worst job in the division, and it uses the same loan data that CASTOR will hold.
g: interest accrual
interest building up day by day on a loan before it is actually paid

lines.text: She is right about the letters. I have signed six hundred of them.
lines.plain: She is right about the letters. I have signed six hundred of them myself.

lines.text: Somebody halfway down the table says it would be mad not to fix them while the platform is open. The room warms to the idea in about forty seconds.
lines.plain: Someone in the middle of the table says it would be foolish not to fix the letters while the platform is being built. Within about forty seconds, the room likes the idea.

lines.text: Next to eight point four million it costs nothing.
lines.plain: Compared with 8.4 million euro, it would cost nothing.

lines.text: It is 11:40. Twenty-one faces, and the ceiling tile, turn to you.
lines.plain: It is 11:40. Twenty-one people, and the video picture of the ceiling, are all looking at you.

choice.prompt: The brainstorm has produced a new deliverable and the room likes it. What do you do?
choice.promptPlain: The open discussion has produced a new deliverable, and the room wants it. What do you do?

options.t: Record it as a proposed change, keep it out of the baseline, and bring the discussion back inside the Charter.
options.tPlain: Write it down as a proposed change. Keep it out of the approved plan. Bring the discussion back inside the Project Charter.

reply.text: Written down, not signed off. Marie, if it survives the assessment you get your letters. If it does not, you will know who said no and why.
reply.plain: It is written down, but not approved. Marie, if it passes the assessment, you get your letters. If it does not, you will know who refused and for what reason.

options.why: The approach discussion may be a brainstorming session, but the guide bounds it: within the limits set by the Project Charter (p.40, step 7). The Charter's scope was accepted by the Project Steering Committee on 24 Mar 2026, so a kick-off cannot enlarge it. Page 41 then obliges you to summarise proposed changes in the Minutes of Meeting and to record them in the relevant log.
options.whyPlain: The guide allows a brainstorm about the approach, but only inside the limits of the Project Charter (page 40, step 7). The Steering Committee accepted that scope on 24 March 2026, so this meeting cannot make the scope bigger. Page 41 then tells you to put proposed changes in the minutes and also in the correct log.
ref: Discuss the overall approach to the project. This discussion can be a brainstorming session within the limits set by the Project Charter.

options.t: Add the interest notices to scope. The room agrees and the Charter is three weeks old.
options.tPlain: Put the interest notices into the project scope. Everyone agrees, and the Charter is only three weeks old.

reply.text: Then put it in writing, because what I took to Lorenzo's board on the twenty-fourth said something else.
reply.plain: Then write it down properly, because the document I took to Lorenzo's board on 24 March said something different.

options.why: Scope agreed in a kick-off is scope nobody has estimated. Project change management exists to bring transparency, accountability and traceability to changes made after the scope and plans are baselined (p.90); a room agreeing quickly at 11:40 supplies none of the three.
options.whyPlain: Scope agreed in a kick-off meeting is scope that nobody has costed. The change process exists to make changes clear, owned and traceable after the scope and plans are approved (page 90). A room agreeing quickly at 11:40 gives you none of that.
ref: Project change management brings transparency, accountability and traceability to all project changes implemented after the project scope and project plans have been baselined.

options.t: Rule the item out of order. The agenda is the agenda and the discussion has drifted.
options.tPlain: Refuse to discuss it. The agenda is fixed and the discussion has gone off the subject.

reply.text: Understood. That is the last idea I bring into one of these rooms.
reply.plain: I understand. That is the last idea I will bring to a meeting like this.

options.why: Wrong in the other direction. Clarifying stakeholder expectations and identifying risks are stated aims of this meeting (p.40), and page 41 requires proposed changes to be minuted. You keep the timetable and lose the User Representative, who is a required participant precisely because she knows what the five days are for.
options.whyPlain: This is wrong the other way. Two stated aims of this meeting are to clarify what stakeholders expect and to find risks (page 40), and page 41 says proposed changes must be minuted. You protect the timetable and lose the User Representative, who is required to attend exactly because she knows what those five days are for.
ref: identify project risks

options.t: Ask Florence to decide now. She is the Project Owner and she owns the benefits.
options.tPlain: Ask Florence to decide immediately. She is the Project Owner and she owns the benefits.

reply.text: I could. I would be deciding on a number that nobody in this room has estimated.
reply.plain: I could decide. But I would be deciding about a cost that nobody in this room has estimated.

options.why: The Project Owner does approve a great deal, including the Project Handbook. She does not approve scope in a room at 11:40 with no assessment behind it: the change plan requires the assessment step and names who may approve at each impact level (p.90, step 6).
options.whyPlain: The Project Owner approves many things, including the Project Handbook. But she does not approve new scope at 11:40 with no assessment. The change plan requires an assessment first, and it names who may approve a change at each level of impact (page 90, step 6).
ref: Define who is responsible for approving changes at the various impact levels, and how this decision is communicated to the rest of the team.

you.o: Project Manager. Responsible for organising and running the Planning Kick-off Meeting.
you.k: Knows the gate closed at 96% on 27 Mar and that no plan yet exists.
you.w: Wants a minute-taker, the Charter walked, and no new deliverable voted in before lunch.
you.f: Afraid that saying no to Curie today costs him her cooperation for two years.

nightingale.o: Project Owner. Accountable for the project's success and for the benefits.
nightingale.k: Knows both audit findings are still open and that Planning runs to 26 Jun.
nightingale.w: Wants the room to hear why this project exists, then wants her morning back.
nightingale.f: Afraid Planning becomes a paper exercise that delays the build by a quarter.

leonardo.o: Solution Provider. Accountable for the deliverables and for contractor performance.
leonardo.k: Knows the procurement timetable ends in a contract award on 18 Sep 2026.
leonardo.w: Wants buy-not-build said out loud, minuted, in front of his own architects.
leonardo.f: Afraid his division quietly starts building a platform he has promised to buy.

hopper.o: Business Manager. Coordinates the Business Implementation Group and supports the PM.
hopper.k: Knows which of her forty administrators can be released and which cannot.
hopper.w: Wants every person in the room placed in a named group before lunch.
hopper.f: Afraid the business side becomes an audience rather than half the project.

curie.o: User Representative. Represents the users and signs off user-related documents.
curie.k: Knows exactly what the five working days in SC1 are actually spent on.
curie.w: Wants half an hour on the quarterly interest notices and a straight answer about SC1.
curie.f: Afraid the one-day target is met by deleting a control she depends on.

gantt.o: Project Support Office. Takes the minutes and administers the project record.
gantt.k: Knows the collateral register lessons learned and where the report is filed.
gantt.w: Wants to know whether he is minuting, and the deputy's name for the attendance list.
gantt.f: Afraid decisions are taken this morning that no document will show next year.

note: Guide check: section 6.1, p.40. The Planning Phase starts with an official Planning Kick-off Meeting whose aims are to ensure everyone understands the project scope, clarify the expectations of all key stakeholders, identify project risks and discuss the project plans. Required participants are the Project Core Team, the Business Implementation Group, the User Representatives, the Solution Provider, the Project Owner and the Business Manager; the Project Manager Assistant and Project Support Office are required if they are part of the project. Before the meeting: plan it, draft the agenda with the points to be discussed, send it in advance, ensure the required people attend. During it: introduce participants, identify a minute-taker, walk the Charter, outline the Planning Phase, describe roles, discuss the timeline, discuss the approach as a brainstorm within the limits set by the Charter, discuss the plans needed, discuss risks, constraints and assumptions, present the supporting tools, take any other business, summarise and state next steps. RASCI: AGB I, PSC A, PO C, BM S, BIG C, SP C, PM R, PCT C. Approver: the Meeting Agenda is not approved; the Project Steering Committee is Accountable for the meeting itself. Pages 40 and 41.
notePlain: Rule: the Planning Phase starts with an official Planning Kick-off Meeting. Its aims are that everyone understands the scope, that stakeholder expectations are clear, that risks are found, and that the project plans are discussed. The core team, the business implementation group, the user representatives, the Solution Provider, the Project Owner and the Business Manager must attend. The support office and any project manager assistant attend too, if the project has them. Before the meeting you plan it, write the agenda, send it early, and make sure the right people come. In the meeting you introduce people, name a minute-taker, walk through the Charter, explain the Planning Phase, describe the roles, discuss the timeline, discuss the approach inside the limits of the Charter, agree which plans are needed, discuss risks and assumptions, show the tools, and close with a summary and next steps. RASCI: Project Manager Responsible, Steering Committee Accountable, Project Owner Consulted, Business Manager supports, and the rest are consulted or informed. Nobody approves the agenda. Pages 40 and 41.

title: The minutes are not the record
where: ESM, Kirchberg — Project Support Office, third floor

lines.text: Friday, twenty past eight. Rain on the glass, a tram sliding past below, and eleven pages of Gantt's handwriting on the table between you.
lines.plain: It is Friday at 08:20. Rain runs down the window and a tram passes below. Eleven pages of Gantt's handwritten notes lie on the table between you.

lines.text: Eleven pages. I can have a full transcript by Monday.
lines.plain: There are eleven pages. I can produce a complete written record by Monday.

lines.text: I do not want a transcript.
lines.plain: I do not want a full written record.

lines.text: Gantt puts the pages down with the flat, careful movement of a man who spent an evening on them.
lines.plain: Gantt puts the pages down slowly and carefully. He clearly spent an evening writing them.

lines.text: Four things. What was raised. What was identified as a risk. What was decided. What somebody proposed to change. Everything else is texture, and I will read the texture in your notebook if I ever need it.
lines.plain: I need four things. The issues that were raised. The risks that were found. The decisions that were taken. The changes that were proposed. Everything else is background detail, and I can read your notebook if I ever need it.
g: Minutes of Meeting
the short official record of a meeting: what was raised, decided and to be done
ref: The Minutes of Meeting (MoM) should include a summary of project issues raised, risks identified, decisions taken and changes proposed.

lines.text: Then the deputy. Finance and Control. Ilona Vas, on the attendance grid, in full.
lines.plain: Then we must record the deputy. She came from Finance and Control. Her name is Ilona Vas, and it goes on the attendance list in full.

lines.text: In full. In two years somebody will ask whether Finance and Control were in the room when the same-day reconciliation criterion was explained.
lines.plain: Yes, in full. In two years somebody will ask whether Finance and Control were present when the same-day reconciliation target was explained.

lines.text: Three risks came out of that room and not one of them is an IT risk. Has anybody noticed that.
lines.plain: Three risks came out of that meeting. None of them is an IT risk. Has anyone noticed that?

lines.text: Ratification of the Treaty reform is not complete, and we have promised to onboard the backstop in six weeks when it is. The parallel run in early 2028 sits next to an EFSF bond rollover. And Lending Operations cannot release its people for two years without something else giving.
lines.plain: First, the Treaty reform is not yet ratified, and we have promised to add the backstop instrument within six weeks once it is. Second, the parallel run in early 2028 falls close to an EFSF bond rollover. Third, Lending Operations cannot release its staff for two years unless something else is dropped.
g: bond rollover
repaying a maturing bond by issuing a new one, so the funding continues
Risk Log
the register of identified risks, with owner, score and planned response

lines.text: Write the third one with names in it. It sounds like weather until it says Marie Curie, forty days.
lines.plain: Write the third risk with names in it. Without names it sounds like bad weather. With them it says Marie Curie, forty days.

lines.text: Good. All three go in the minutes.
lines.plain: Good. All three risks go into the minutes.

lines.text: In the minutes and in the logs. The minutes summarise a morning. The Risk, Issue and Decision Logs are the registers, and they have been open since January.
lines.plain: They go in the minutes and in the logs. The minutes are a summary of one morning. The Risk Log, the Issue Log and the Decision Log are the real registers, and they have been open since January.
ref: Note that the issues, risks, decisions and project changes should also be recorded in the relevant logs.

lines.text: And the interest notices? There is no Change Log.
lines.plain: And what about the interest notices? We do not have a Change Log.

lines.text: There is as of this week. Status Submitted, which is where every change starts, and from this morning Marie's letters are an entry with a number rather than an idea somebody had at a whiteboard.
lines.plain: We have one from this week. The status is Submitted, which is the first status of every change. From this morning, Marie's letters are a numbered entry, not just an idea from a whiteboard.
g: Change Log
the register of requested changes, their assessment and the decision taken on each
ref: Submitted: This is the initial status. Use this while the requested change is still being specified.

lines.text: Florence reads the draft standing up, coat still on, on her way to a Board of Directors briefing at nine.
lines.plain: Florence reads the draft while standing, still wearing her coat. She is on her way to a Board of Directors briefing at 09:00.

lines.text: If I sign this, what have I approved?
lines.plain: If I sign this document, what am I approving?

lines.text: Nothing. It records what happened.
lines.plain: Nothing. It only records what happened.

lines.text: What the room agreed the project needs — the list of plans, the tailoring, the escalation rules — becomes the Handbook. That is the one you approve, and I would like it in front of you before the end of the month.
lines.plain: What the room agreed the project needs — the list of plans, the tailoring decisions and the escalation rules — goes into the Project Handbook. That is the document you approve, and I would like you to have it before the end of the month.
ref: Use the minutes from the Planning Kick-off Meeting as a basis for defining the Project Handbook.

lines.text: Then send it to everyone on the Charter's list, not only the people who turned up. Half my division learns what is happening from documents they were copied into.
lines.plain: Then send the minutes to everyone on the stakeholder list in the Charter, not only to those who attended. Half of my division finds out what is happening from documents they were copied into.
ref: Distribute the Minutes of Meeting (MoM) to the appropriate stakeholders (as identified in the Project Charter).

lines.text: That is eighty-one addresses.
lines.plain: That is eighty-one email addresses.

lines.text: Eighty-one.
lines.plain: Yes. Eighty-one.

lines.text: She is gone before the door finishes closing. Gantt is already deleting the transcript he wrote on Thursday evening, page by page, without comment.
lines.plain: She leaves before the door has closed. Gantt is already deleting the full record he wrote on Thursday evening, page by page, and says nothing about it.

lines.text: Six actions, six owners, six dates. Four of them are yours.
lines.plain: There are six actions, six owners and six due dates. Four of the actions belong to you.

lines.text: Five. I have just taken the eighty-one addresses.
lines.plain: Five actions. I have just accepted the job of sending it to eighty-one people.

lines.text: The Minutes of Meeting go out at 16:40, one working day after the meeting. Nobody replies until Tuesday, and the reply is from Legal, who could not see the screen.
lines.plain: The minutes are sent at 16:40, one working day after the meeting. Nobody replies until Tuesday. The only reply is from Legal, who could not see the screen during the meeting.

you.o: Project Manager. Responsible for the Minutes of Meeting and for their distribution.
you.k: Knows the kick-off produced three risks, three decisions and one proposed change.
you.w: Wants a four-part summary today, not a transcript on Monday.
you.f: Afraid the proposed change survives only in Gantt's notebook and reappears as a promise.

gantt.o: Project Support Office. Minute-taker for the kick-off; keeps the logs and the repository.
gantt.k: Knows who was present, including the deputy nobody else can name.
gantt.w: Wants his eleven pages to count for something after an evening spent on them.
gantt.f: Afraid a summary drops the one sentence that matters in 2028.

hopper.o: Business Manager. Supports the Project Manager and owns the client-side risks.
hopper.k: Knows exactly how many days each of her administrators can give the project.
hopper.w: Wants the staffing risk written with named people and real numbers of days.
hopper.f: Afraid an abstract risk is easy for everyone to agree with and ignore.

nightingale.o: Project Owner. Will approve the Project Handbook; approves nothing today.
nightingale.k: Knows the kick-off happened and has not yet read a word of the plans.
nightingale.w: Wants to know what her signature commits her to before she puts it anywhere.
nightingale.f: Afraid her division hears about its own project through forwarded email.

note: Guide check: section 6.1, p.41. After the Planning Kick-off Meeting the Minutes of Meeting are distributed to the appropriate stakeholders, as identified in the Project Charter — not merely to the attendance list. The Minutes must include a summary of project issues raised, risks identified, decisions taken and changes proposed. The guide then adds the rule beginners skip: those issues, risks, decisions and project changes should also be recorded in the relevant logs. The Minutes are a summary; the Risk, Issue, Decision and Change Logs are the registers. The Risk, Issue and Decision Logs are set up during Initiating, the Change Log typically during Planning (p.31), and a new change enters the Change Log with the initial status Submitted (p.96). The Planning Kick-off Minutes of Meeting are a named input to the Project Handbook (p.42). RASCI: none — PM² gives no RASCI row for the Minutes of Meeting artefact; the meeting has one, the document does not. Approver: nobody. Page 41.
notePlain: Rule: after the Planning Kick-off Meeting the minutes go to the stakeholders named in the Project Charter, not only to the people who attended. The minutes must summarise four things: issues raised, risks found, decisions taken and changes proposed. The guide adds a rule that beginners forget: those same four things must also be written into the correct logs. The minutes are a summary. The Risk Log, Issue Log, Decision Log and Change Log are the real registers. The Risk, Issue and Decision Logs are opened during Initiating, and the Change Log during Planning (page 31). A new change enters the Change Log with the first status, Submitted (page 96). The Planning Kick-off minutes are a listed input to the Project Handbook (page 42). There is no RASCI row for the minutes and nobody approves them. Page 41.

title: The book everyone will ignore, correctly
where: ESM, Kirchberg — Florence Nightingale's office, Lending Operations

lines.text: Forty-one pages, printed, because Florence does not read long documents on a screen. There is a sandwich on her desk that she has not opened since half past twelve.
lines.plain: The draft Project Handbook is 41 pages, printed, because Florence will not read long documents on a screen. A sandwich has been on her desk since 12:30 and she has not opened it.

lines.text: Forty-one pages of what?
lines.plain: Forty-one pages about what?

lines.text: How we run this. Not what we build.
lines.plain: How we will run this project. Not what we will build.

lines.text: Approach, the controlling processes, the rules, the escalation route, and who holds which role. The what is the Charter, and then the Work Plan in June.
lines.plain: It covers the approach, the control processes, the project rules, the escalation route, and who holds which role. What we build is in the Charter, and later in the Work Plan in June.
g: Project Handbook
the document that says how a project will be run: approach, processes, rules, roles
ref: The Project Handbook summarises the project objectives and documents the selected approach for achieving the project goals.

lines.text: Give me the one page I would read if I read one.
lines.plain: Tell me the single page I should read, if I only read one.

lines.text: Two point two. Three critical success factors. Lending Operations releases its people for the whole build. You are visibly the owner of this. SC1 to SC5 are still measurable in 2028.
lines.plain: Section 2.2. It lists three critical success factors. First, Lending Operations releases its staff for the whole build. Second, you are visibly the owner of the project. Third, the five success criteria can still be measured in 2028.
g: Critical Success Factor
a condition that must hold or the project cannot succeed, whatever else goes well
ref: Identify Critical Success Factors (CSFs) and define important project management objectives.

lines.text: The first one is a promise about my staffing plan, not about your project.
lines.plain: The first one is a promise about my staffing plan. It is not about your project.

lines.text: Which is why it is up there and not in a wish list at the back.
lines.plain: That is exactly why it is at the front of the document and not in a list of hopes at the back.

lines.text: Leonardo has been drawing on his copy since he sat down. He turns it round. The project lifecycle, redrawn, with the four phases as nested arcs and the gates as narrow points between them.
lines.plain: Since sitting down, Leonardo has been drawing on his copy. He turns it round to show it. He has redrawn the project lifecycle, with the four phases as curved shapes and the gates as narrow points between them.

lines.text: Yours is a row of boxes. A gate is not a box, it is a narrowing.
lines.plain: Your version is a row of boxes. But a gate is not a box. It is a narrow point.

lines.text: It is a beautiful drawing and it is not going in the Handbook.
lines.plain: It is a beautiful drawing, and it will not go into the Handbook.

lines.text: No. Probably not. Three point two, then. Explain the tailoring table, because I count six management plans and four documents.
lines.plain: No. Probably not. Then let us look at section 3.2. Explain the tailoring table. I count six management plans, but only four documents.
g: tailoring
adjusting the method to the project: which plans are separate documents and which are short sections

lines.text: Requirements, issue, quality and communications each get their own document. Risk and change stay as sections 4.1 and 4.4, because a section is enough for them here and a separate plan would only be read by me.
lines.plain: The requirements, issue, quality and communications plans each get their own document. The risk and change plans stay as sections 4.1 and 4.4 of the Handbook. A section is enough for them on this project, and a separate document would only be read by me.
ref: When sufficient, a brief definition of each management process or plan can be provided in the Project Handbook.

lines.text: That is a shortcut.
lines.plain: That is a shortcut.

lines.text: It is a decision, written where you can argue with it. You are arguing with it now, which is the point.
lines.plain: It is a decision, and it is written down where you can challenge it. You are challenging it right now, which is exactly the purpose.
ref: All Project Management Plans should be considered part of the Project Handbook.

lines.text: Read three point five out. I want them to hear it before it matters rather than after.
lines.plain: Please read section 3.5 aloud. I want everyone to hear it before it becomes important, not afterwards.

note: Guide check: section 6.3, pp.44–45. The Project Stakeholder Matrix lists all key stakeholders with their contact details and clearly states their role or roles in the project, and may also classify or categorise them. The Project Manager prepares it; the Business Manager assists, particularly with identifying stakeholders on the client side; other stakeholders are consulted. Inputs are the Business Case, the Project Charter and the Planning Kick-off Minutes of Meeting. The two steps are to identify everyone who will have a role using the organisation's structure, and to assign each of them a specific project role for the project's duration, based on the standard PM² roles. The guide warns explicitly that all applicable regulations on privacy and personal data rights must be respected when establishing and handling the matrix. The classification technique behind the columns is the Stakeholder Interest/Influence Matrix (Appendix C.3, p.101): interest is the degree of enthusiasm the stakeholder shows — positive, neutral or negative — while influence is their power over the planning and implementation of activities, and it warns that the document names people and must be kept confidential. notePlain: Rule: the Project Stakeholder Matrix lists every key stakeholder, their contact details and their role in the project. It may also group or rate them. The Project Manager writes it. The Business Manager helps, above all with finding the stakeholders on the business side. Other stakeholders are consulted. Its inputs are the Business Case, the Project Charter and the Planning Kick-off minutes. There are two steps: use the organisation structure to find everyone with a role, then give each person a specific project role for the whole project, based on the standard PM2 roles. The guide states clearly that privacy and personal-data rules must be respected when building and handling the matrix. The rating columns come from the Stakeholder Interest/Influence technique (page 101). Interest means how enthusiastic a person is: positive, neutral or negative. Influence means the power they hold over planning and doing the work. The guide also warns that the document names real people and must be kept confidential. RASCI: Project Manager Responsible, Project Owner Accountable, Business Manager supports, core team and business group consulted, and the rest informed. Approver: the Project Owner. note: Guide check: Appendix B.1 and B.2, pp.89–90. The Requirements Management Plan defines the requirements management approach, process steps, responsibilities, tools, techniques and artefacts; the requirements themselves are documented and managed in separate artefacts such as a requirements matrix. It defines what a requirement is and the possible states of its lifecycle, names the prioritisation techniques used — MoSCoW among them — and must be aligned with the change management process, with requirement changes traced to deliverables and activities. In the absence of a more specialised role, the Project Manager executes the process from initiation until all requirements are implemented and validated. RASCI: AGB I, PSC I, PO A, BM C, BIG C, SP I, PM R, PCT S — the only management plan where the Project Core Team supports. The Project Change Management Plan defines the activities, roles and responsibilities for identifying, documenting, assessing, approving, prioritising, implementing, controlling and communicating changes, and brings transparency, accountability and traceability to changes made after the scope and plans are baselined. It defines who approves at each impact level, and the Change Log documents every requested change and traces the related decisions and actions; its statuses include Submitted, Assessing, Waiting for approval, Approved, Rejected, Postponed, Merged and Implemented (p.96). RASCI: AGB I, PSC I, PO A, BM C, BIG I, SP I, PM R, PCT I. Approver of both: the Project Owner. Pages 89, 90 and 96.
notePlain: Rule: the Requirements Management Plan says how requirements are handled. It covers the approach, the process steps, who does what, and the tools and documents used. The requirements themselves live in a separate document, such as a requirements matrix. The plan defines what counts as a requirement and the states it can be in. It names the ranking techniques used, including MoSCoW. It must fit the change process, and requirement changes must be traceable to deliverables and activities. If there is no specialist role, the Project Manager runs the process until every requirement is built and validated. In its RASCI the core team supports, which happens in no other management plan. The Project Change Management Plan says how changes are found, described, assessed, approved, ranked, built, controlled and communicated. It makes changes after the baseline clear, owned and traceable. It says who may approve a change at each level of impact. The Change Log records each requested change and its decisions. Its statuses are Submitted, Assessing, Waiting for approval, Approved, Rejected, Postponed, Merged and Implemented (page 96). note: Guide check: section 6.4.1, p.47. The Work Breakdown is the first of the Project Work Plan's three parts. It breaks the project into smaller, more manageable components — deliverables, work packages, activities and tasks — over multiple levels, each with progressively more detailed deliverables and work; its inputs are the Business Case, the Project Charter and the project requirements. Appendix C.6 (p.102) explains why deliverables come first: the Deliverables Breakdown Structure defines what the project will produce, and the Work Breakdown Structure defines the work needed to produce it. Page 46 requires the Project Work Plan to capture all project-related work identified in Planning or emerging in Executing, including risks, issues and corrective actions — so a risk response that costs real effort is a work package, not a footnote. Two plans meet here and are routinely confused. The Transition Plan covers moving from the pre-project to the post-project state: PM = Responsible, PSC = Accountable, and all transition activities become part of the Project Work Plan (p.51). The Business Implementation Plan covers the impact on processes, culture and people and the change-management activities around them: the Business Manager prepares it, the Project Manager only assists and updates the Work Plan to include its activities, RASCI BM = R, PO = A, PM = S (p.52). Different documents, different authors, different approvers — and both sets of activities are scheduled and controlled inside the one Project Work Plan. Pages 46, 47, 51, 52 and 102.
notePlain: Rule: the Work Breakdown is the first of the three parts of the Project Work Plan. It splits the project into smaller pieces: deliverables, then work packages, then activities, then tasks. Each level shows more detail. Its inputs are the Business Case, the Project Charter and the project requirements. Page 102 explains why you list deliverables first: the deliverables structure says what the project will produce, and the work structure says what work produces it. Page 46 says the Work Plan must hold all project work, including work that comes from risks, issues and corrective actions. So a risk response that costs real effort is a work package, not a note. Two plans meet here and people often confuse them. The Transition Plan covers moving from the old state to the new one. The Project Manager writes it and the Steering Committee approves it, and all its activities go into the Work Plan. The Business Implementation Plan covers the effect on processes, culture and people, and the change work around them. The Business Manager writes it, the Project Owner approves it, and the Project Manager only assists and adds its activities to the Work Plan. Different documents, different authors, different approvers, and one Work Plan holding both sets of activities. Pages 46, 47, 51, 52 and 102.

note: Guide check: section 6.4, p.46. The Project Work Plan elaborates the project scope, identifies and organises the work and deliverables, and establishes the basis for estimating duration, calculating resources and scheduling the work; once scheduled it becomes the basis for monitoring progress and controlling the project. It has three parts in fixed order: Work Breakdown, then Effort and Cost Estimates, then Project Schedule. Section 6.4.2 gives the rule that catches beginners — after a task is assigned to a resource or to a resource profile it also becomes possible to calculate its cost — so estimating and costing are one movement, not two exercises months apart. Section 6.4.3 makes the schedule the instrument the Project Manager uses to authorise, coordinate and accept project work and to monitor overall progress. The plan must be baselined and kept up to date for the life of the project. RASCI: AGB I, PSC A, PO C, BM S/C, BIG C, SP C, PM R, PCT S/C. Approver: the Project Steering Committee — not the Project Owner, who is only Consulted. Watch the guide's own role lists on p.25: the Project Steering Committee approves key artefacts including the Project Work Plan, while the Project Owner's list also names the Work Plan. Where they collide the artefact's RASCI table decides, and it says PSC. With the Project Handbook and Project Stakeholder Matrix approved by the Project Owner, and the Project Work Plan and Quality Management Plan approved by the Project Steering Committee on 26 Jun 2026, CASTOR is one week from the Ready for Executing gate on 03 Jul 2026. Pages 46, 47, 25 and 102.
notePlain: Rule: the Project Work Plan develops the scope, organises the work and the deliverables, and gives the basis for estimating time, working out resources and building the schedule. Once scheduled, it is what you monitor progress against. It has three parts, in this order: the Work Breakdown, then the Effort and Cost Estimates, then the Schedule. One rule catches beginners: as soon as a task is given to a person or a resource profile, you can calculate its cost. So estimating effort and costing it are one step, not two separate exercises. The schedule is the tool the Project Manager uses to authorise work, coordinate it, accept it and track progress. The plan must be baselined and kept up to date for the whole project. When they disagree, the artefact's RASCI table decides, and it says the Steering Committee. With the Handbook and the Stakeholder Matrix approved by the Project Owner, and the Work Plan and the Quality Management Plan approved by the Steering Committee on 26 June 2026, CASTOR is one week away from the Ready for Executing gate on 3 July 2026.
